analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal institute to develop medicines, hold the patents, and sell them at cost.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2026 and referred to two House committees; no committee or floor action has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new National Institute for Biomedical Research and Development inside the National Institutes of Health, funded with $90 billion, to develop drugs, biologics, and medical devices from start to finish. The federal government would own the patents on anything it developed or funded, license them broadly (free to public and nonprofit entities), manufacture medicines publicly where possible, and sell them at cost. The bill also bans pharmaceutical company lobbyists and executives from the institute's governing board and requires all trial data to be published openly.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who cannot afford brand-name drug prices, including people on Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance; public health programs that would see lower drug costs; generic and nonprofit manufacturers who would get free licenses to federally funded inventions; and researchers who would get open access to trial data. The bill prioritizes unmet public health needs over commercial return.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a new NIH institute to run full-cycle development of drugs, devices, and biologics, with the stated purposes of promoting long-term access to medicines and making them available at equitable and accessible prices [S2].

Requires the federal government to own the patents and trade secrets on any product developed or funded by the institute, and bars the government from claiming trade secrets or confidential commercial information on those products [S2].

Provides for public manufacturing of federally patented drugs sold at cost, and where public manufacturing is not practicable, licenses patents to nonprofits before for-profits, with non-exclusive terms, cost-plus pricing, and free licenses to public and nonprofit entities [S2].

Gives the government a right of first refusal on inventions from NIH-funded research, conditions all HHS extramural biomedical research funding on handing over data and manufacturing know-how needed for technology transfer, and sets a default policy of licensing institute patents to the Medicines Patent Pool [S2].

Requires the institute to publish all safety and effectiveness data submitted in FDA applications, trial data, costs, licensing agreements, and contracts, and to conduct transparent health technology assessments of its products [S2].

Bars registered pharmaceutical-manufacturer lobbyists and senior executives of companies under federal enforcement settlements from serving on the governing board, and requires at least four board members to be civil society representatives and patient advocates from organizations independent of industry funding [S2].
Prioritizes research spending based on public health impact and unmet needs rather than commercial potential [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through a $90 billion authorization for fiscal year 2027 that remains available until spent [S2]. Brand-name pharmaceutical and biotech companies would face competition from publicly owned, at-cost medicines and from free or non-exclusive licenses to inventions built on publicly funded research, reducing revenue on products where the government funded development.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $90 billion for fiscal year 2027 with no revenue offset, so it would add directly to federal spending unless Congress separately raises the money [S2].

Drug development has a high failure rate: most candidates entering full-cycle development never reach the market, so a large share of the public investment would buy nothing a patient could use, and a government institute would take on risks that private firms currently absorb.

Because the government would own patents and manufacturing know-how on products it funded, private companies would have weaker incentives to invest in research in areas the institute covers, and some firms might avoid HHS-funded research altogether to keep their intellectual property, which could slow some private innovation.

The bill requires publication of all FDA application data without trade secret protection for institute-funded products, which companies would treat as a significant concession of commercially valuable information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the program worked as written, patients and public health programs would gain permanently lower-priced medicines, and $90 billion is roughly in the range of what the government already loses each year to brand-name drug prices above what other wealthy countries pay, so a well-run program could plausibly pay for itself. But the bill is ambitious and untested: the same investment could yield few approved products, and it creates a large new federal operation with no funding offset and few guardrails on cost overruns. The transparency and conflict-of-interest provisions are unusually strong, which is where the design is most solid.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on March 5, 2026, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the Medicines for the People Act on March 5, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S4].
The bill has four cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been recorded since the referral [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: the bill sits in committee, so brand-name drug makers keep the current pricing structure and patients keep current prices for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 5, 2026 and became its sole lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Summer Lee (PA) and Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (FL)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill ended with four Democratic cosponsors total.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship is Democratic (one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors); no Republicans have signed on and no committee action has occurred [S3].

industries.note: The bill gives the government ownership of patents on publicly funded drug development, licenses them to the Medicines Patent Pool and others at little or no cost, and sells medicines at cost, which would create public-domain competition for brand-name products and strip trade secret protection from institute-funded products. It would reduce revenue precisely where the public is paying the most.

The bill requires free licenses to public and nonprofit entities, gives nonprofits preference over for-profits for manufacturing, and hands over complete manufacturing documentation, making these firms the production channel for affordable medicines.

industries.industry: Contract research organizations and academic research contractors
industries.note: The institute would contract with public and private entities for research and development under a $90 billion authorization, and the bill requires contractors to share their data openly, limiting what companies can keep proprietary. Their gain is real but conditioned on surrendering intellectual property rights.

The bill makes federal labs the permanent home of full-cycle public drug development, with authority to acquire land and build facilities, and to take rights to inventions from NIH-funded research. Public money and staff would flow through this new federal channel indefinitely.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has only four Democratic cosponsors, has been double-referred to two committees, and has seen no hearings or markups since its March 2026 introduction. Bills at this stage with this level of support rarely reach the floor, especially ones authorizing $90 billion in new spending; it will most likely remain in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress.
